title: Va'etchanan: at home and on the way (Deuteronomy 6:7)
hook: talk of them sitting at home, walking by the way, lying down and rising up
carry: at home and on the way
tomorrow: Va'etchanan: the right and the good (Deuteronomy 6:18)

segments.voice: Yesterday, v'ahavta: love with both hearts, your life and your might. Your line was with all your heart. What did you bring that you usually hold back? Today, where those words are meant to live. Day four hundred ninety.

The real conversations in a family often happen sideways. Not always at the formal dinner. Sometimes in the car, eyes on the road, when nobody has to look at anybody. Or at the edge of a bed, lights off, when a kid suddenly asks the big question. Or in the kitchen at seven in the morning, half awake. The paragraph after the Shema seems to know this. It doesn't schedule a weekly lesson. It names four ordinary places where words can be spoken, and an ordinary day already passes through them.
screen: `IN THE CAR, EYES ON THE ROAD.` → `THE EDGE OF THE BED.` → `FOUR ORDINARY PLACES.`

segments.voice: The verse, in the old Jewish translation: "and thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children, and shalt talk of them when thou sittest in thy house, and when thou walkest by the way, and when thou liest down, and when thou risest up." Teach them diligently is one Hebrew word, v'shinantam, and early readers hear sharpen in it, while others hear repeat. Say it until it's sharp. And talk of them, v'dibarta bam: not preach, talk. Then the four places. Sitting at home, walking on the road, lying down, rising up. The rabbis read the last pair as times. That's why the Shema is said at night and in the morning. But they argued about the posture. The Mishnah records it. The school of Shammai said: at night, recline, and in the morning, stand, because the verse says lying down and rising up. The school of Hillel said: everyone says it in their own way, however they happen to be, because the verse also says when thou walkest by the way. Read that way, the verse isn't asking you to arrange your body for the words. It's asking the words to come along wherever your body already is. The Mishnah even tells of Rabbi Tarfon, who lay down by the road at night to follow Shammai's ruling and put himself in danger from robbers. His colleagues told him he deserved what nearly happened, for setting aside Hillel's view.
screen: `V'SHINANTAM: SHARPEN, REPEAT.` · `TALK, DON'T PREACH.` · `LYING DOWN AND RISING: NIGHT AND MORNING.` · `HILLEL: AS YOU ARE, ON THE WAY.` · then, large: `AT HOME AND ON THE WAY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: talk about something that matters. Settle, and breathe. Think of the four places in your own day: home, the road, bedtime, the morning. Which one is quietest? Which one has another person in it? Pick one, and pick one thing that matters to you that you haven't said in a while. A value, a hope, a worry, a story. Not a speech. A sentence or two, said where you already are. The bell holds the time.
Va'etchanan. And I pleaded. The portion that holds the Shema, and the four places its words are meant to travel.

Your line: at home and on the way. This week: eicha, the scouts, the gentle march, a pleading, a memory, the Shema, and now its places. Today, say one thing that matters in the car, the kitchen, or at bedtime. Day four hundred ninety.

howItsDone: Jews say the Shema at night and in the morning, following the verse's lying down and rising up, and Jewish law follows the school of Hillel that it may be said in whatever position one happens to be.

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): hook no longer opens 'Think about'; the debated root of v'shinantam is now given as readers' views, not fact.
Deuteronomy 6:7 quoted from JPS 1917 from memory; verify.

Mishnah Berakhot 1:3: Shammai and Hillel on posture; Rabbi Tarfon lay down on the road, was in danger from bandits, and was told he deserved to be harmed for transgressing the words of Beit Hillel; softened in the script ('deserved what nearly happened'); confirm.
The root of v'shinantam (shanan, to sharpen; Sifrei links it to sharp words; others link it to shanah, repeat) is debated; both given.
